segments.text: This demo compares SHA-3-256, the compact core in this project, and Oxide's quartz implementation.
Here's how the input architecture changes speed and resource use.
Follow the two architectures from input to digest.
Oxide's Quartz Core receives one byte per clock through the local adapter.
Those bytes fill two block buffers, each 136 bytes wide.
One buffer fills while the other feeds the Kekak state.
After 24 permutation rounds, the result is copied into a separate digest register.
Double buffering keeps the byte stream input moving.

chapters.title: Compact: absorb directly into the state

segments.text: Now keep that reference above and look at the changes below.
The compact core accepts the full 8-byte DMA bead into a small buffer.
An aligned exclusive ore feeds it directly into the hash state.
The two full block buffers are gone.
The digest also reads directly from the held state, removing another register.
The outlined blocks show where storage and input logic changed.
Capture and absorption still use separate cycles.
The 24-round permutation is unchanged.
There are two more refinements inside the compact core. Compared with the
earlier wide version, padding uses static decoding in the 17 rate lanes, instead of
selecting across all 25 state lanes. Framing checks are registered before they
control state updates. These changes reduce surrounding logic without
changing the simulated cycle count. The separate standalone synthesis comparison
drops from 5,664 lookup tables to 4,498.
Here are the routed SHA-3 256 resource counts.
About 23% fewer lookup tables, 58% fewer flip-flops.
Those totals include the local adapters, so the comparison covers the complete routed hash partitions.
Both use zero block RAM and zero DSP blocks.
Both cores use the same board, shell, driver, and 100 MHz clock.
The comparison uses the median of 7 samples after warm-up, with every digest checked against software.
Upload and reconfiguration are outside these timers.
Now compare SHA-3 256 hashing time for a 16.8 megabyte message.
Oxide's quartz takes about 169 milliseconds.
The compact core takes 72.
That's 2.36 times the DMA throughput.
Through the processing system API, the gain is 1.91 times,
with copying and request overheads still included.

chapters.title: Why small messages can favor Oxide

segments.text: At 64 bytes, software and DMA setup dominate the request.
The wider input path has very little data to accelerate.
Quartz had the lower median here, but the sample ranges overlap.
Request overhead and run-to-run variation can outweigh the streaming gain.
Higher bulk throughput doesn't guarantee lower latency for a tiny request.
The reserved region and image size are unchanged.
Power and oxide production system performance weren't measured.
Thanks to Oxide and the Quartz contributors for making the reference available.
Their unchanged source and license are retained alongside the measurements.
The project was developed with AI assistance.
Now, onto the board.

chapters.title: Same file, both physical SHA3-256 cores

segments.text: Now run both SHA-3 256 cores from the same dashboard.
Check the board, choose the 16.8 megabyte sample, and enable the core comparison.
One file, two implementation.
The file travels over USB and is verified in the board's memory.
Those transfer seconds are outside the hash timer.
The dashboard loads Oxide's quartz core first, then the compact core.
Each gets a warm-up and seven measured runs through the same local API.
Here are the two results side by side.
Oxide's time is on the left.
The Compact Core's time is on the right.
The file is identical, and both hardware digests match the independent PC reference.
That is the architecture change made visible, less input storage and less time hashing this large file.
